newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's hands seen tied in defence of the yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan's hands seen tied in defence of the yen.

text.p: The dollar is likely to continue its rise against the yen as markets bet that Japan's hands are tied in its efforts to prop up its currency -- unable to sell dollars or raise interest rates.

"If Japan sells dollars for yen in heavy volume and then backs up the action with an interest rate rise, the current weak yen trend will be effectively reversed," said Shuji Ayabe, head of the foreign exchange department at Fuji Bank Ltd.
"But this time it won't be able to do both," he added.

The dollar tumbled against the yen on Friday after hitting a 47-month high of 120.20 yen in Tokyo, after a report that the Bank of Japan had intervened to stop the dollar's sharp rise, although many traders were sceptical about the report.
The dollar was at 119.15 yen in late trade in Tokyo on Monday.
Traders said the greenback remained bullish despite the intervention scare, on steady purchases by investors who are pursuing better returns from investments overseas.
"The dollar could eventually head towards 125 yen, although the pace of its rise may slow," said Takeshi Chujo, a customer dealer at Banque Paribas in Tokyo.
Dealers said currency intervention could be effective, but only if consistent with the economic outlook and credit policy.
Japan's financial heavyweights have repeatedly tried to reassure markets that their economic gloom was undeserved.

On Sunday, influential Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara told a television interviewer that Japan's economy has been performing better than the markets think, and urged Japanese investors to stop selling out their own markets.
The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has stuck to its assessment of a gradual economic recovery in a report published last week.
But traders said there was a gap in the perception of the health of the economy between the market and the official view.

They said despite its brave face, the BOJ would be hard-pressed to raise its rock-bottom official discount rate anytime soon, faced with a fragile stock market and uncertainty over the economy's direction after April's tax revisions, when the consumption tax will go to five percent from three percent and a special income tax cut will end.
Higher interest rates usually make a country's currency more attractive because of a rise in returns from investments.
And the intervention tactic is also unlikely, traders said.

The BOJ should remain wary of a sustained dollar selling policy, partly because such sales would imply a selloff of U.S. Treasuries assets and might have a significant impact on U.S. government bond prices, a Goldman Sachs (Japan) report said.
A resulting rise in U.S. interest rates, coupled with inflationary pressure in the U.S. economy, would also cause damage to the jittery U.S. stock market.

In order to sell dollars for yen in the open market, Japan, the world's biggest foreign reserve holder of $217.87 billion at the end of December, would have to liquidate their foreign assets, mostly short-term U.S. Treasury bills and notes.
Then there is the problem of international coordination.

Japan is the only member among the Group of Seven (G7) nations to voice concern about the recent strength of the dollar. So it may have to act alone discreetly to stop the dollar's rise against the yen for now.
"Dollar sales by Japan will not be justified (internationally) unless, for instance, Tokyo stocks keep falling and that starts affecting other markets overseas," said Fuji Bank's Ayabe.
Dealers say it will be difficult for Japan to draw out a specific agreement to rectify the dollar's rise against the yen at a meeting of G7 nations on February 8 in Berlin.

"The dollar is rising not only against the yen but also against European units, so it would be impossible to come up with a specific measure to deal with only the yen's fall," said Kazunori Iida, foreign exchange department manager at Nissho Iwai Corp.
